title: Stuffy Nose After Drinking: Why It Happens and How to Stop It
excerpt: Why alcohol gives you a stuffy, runny, or sneezy nose, why red wine and beer are the usual triggers, what actually helps, and when nasal symptoms need a doctor.
metaDescription: Why alcohol gives you a stuffy or runny nose and makes you sneeze, why wine and beer are the worst triggers, what helps, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The answer first:** a stuffy, runny, or sneezy nose after drinking is very common and usually harmless. It happens because alcohol widens the blood vessels inside your nose, and because histamine, a chemical your body uses in allergic reactions, rises after you drink. Wine and beer bring their own histamine with them, and alcohol also makes your body release more and clear it more slowly. That's why the stuffiness often shows up within minutes of the first glass, why red wine is the usual suspect, and why clear spirits tend to bother people less.

**What helps most:** switch to clear spirits or drink less of the drink that sets you off, rinse with saline, raise your head at night, and be careful with medicines. Antihistamines and decongestants can help some people, but both interact with alcohol, so check with a pharmacist first. If drinking also causes wheezing, chest tightness, or swelling of the face or lips, that is not ordinary congestion and needs medical care.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Get emergency care (call 911 in the US) if** you have wheezing, chest tightness, or trouble breathing after drinking; swelling of the lips, tongue, face, or throat; widespread hives; or you feel faint or dizzy with a racing heart. **Book a regular appointment if** nasal symptoms happen every time you drink or are getting worse; you have asthma, nasal polyps, or chronic sinus problems; you've ever reacted badly to aspirin or ibuprofen; or you get a blocked nose along with flushing, headaches, or a fast heartbeat after even a small amount of alcohol.

## Why Alcohol Gives You a Stuffy Nose

The inside of your nose is lined with soft tissue that is packed with blood vessels. Those vessels swell and shrink all day long. When they swell, the tissue thickens and the airway narrows, which is what "stuffy" actually is. You don't need extra mucus to feel blocked. Swollen tissue alone is enough.

Alcohol pushes on that system from several directions at once. Most people who notice nasal symptoms after drinking have more than one of these going on.

### 1. Alcohol widens blood vessels

Alcohol is a vasodilator, which means it relaxes the walls of blood vessels so they open wider. It's the same effect that makes some people's cheeks go warm and pink after a drink. In the nose, wider vessels mean more blood in the nasal lining, the lining swells, and air has less room to pass. This effect happens with any type of alcohol, which is why even vodka can make some people a little stuffy if they drink enough of it.

### 2. Histamine in the drink itself

Histamine is a natural compound your immune system uses to trigger allergy symptoms: sneezing, itching, a runny nose, and swollen nasal tissue. It is also made by yeast and bacteria during fermentation. That means fermented drinks, especially wine and some beers, contain histamine and related compounds called biogenic amines before they ever reach you.

Red wine generally carries more histamine than white wine, partly because of the way it is made, with longer contact with grape skins and, in many cases, a second fermentation step. Levels vary a lot from bottle to bottle, so one red may bother you while another doesn't. Distilled spirits contain far less, because distillation leaves most of these compounds behind.

### 3. Alcohol makes your body release and keep more histamine

Here is the part that surprises people. It isn't only the histamine in the glass. When your liver breaks alcohol down, the first product is **acetaldehyde**, a toxic chemical that your body then clears with an enzyme called ALDH2. Acetaldehyde can prompt mast cells (the immune cells that store histamine) to release it. Alcohol also appears to slow the enzyme your gut uses to break down histamine from food and drink, called diamine oxidase or DAO.

Put those together and you get a stacking effect: the histamine you drink, plus the histamine you release, cleared more slowly than usual. For someone whose nose is already sensitive, that's enough to tip them into sneezing and congestion.

### 4. Sulfites and other ingredients

Sulfites are preservatives used in most wines and some beers and ciders. A small number of people, most of them with asthma, are genuinely sensitive to sulfites and can react with wheezing and chest tightness. Whether sulfites cause nasal stuffiness in people without asthma is less clear. They get blamed for a lot (we look at the evidence in our guide to [sulfites in wine](/never-hungover/sulfites-in-wine-headaches)), and histamine is usually the more likely culprit for the nose. Other ingredients can matter too: grapes, wheat, barley, hops, yeast, and the fruit flavorings in ciders and mixers.

### 5. A slow-working ALDH2 enzyme

Many people of East Asian descent, and some people from other backgrounds, carry a gene variant that makes ALDH2 work poorly. Acetaldehyde builds up quickly, causing the well-known red face, a racing heart, nausea, and often a blocked nose. If your stuffiness comes with flushing after one drink, read our full guide to the [alcohol flush reaction](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive), because the nose is the smaller part of that story. Acetaldehyde build-up is a health concern in its own right, not just a cosmetic one.

## Stuffy Nose vs Runny Nose vs Sneezing After Drinking

These symptoms often come together, but they have slightly different causes, and knowing which one you get can point you to the likely trigger.

| Symptom | What's happening | Most common triggers |
|---|---|---|
| Stuffy or blocked nose | Swollen blood vessels in the nasal lining | Any alcohol (vessel widening), plus histamine |
| Runny nose | Histamine making glands and vessels leak fluid | Wine and beer, especially red wine |
| Sneezing | Histamine irritating nerve endings in the nose | Wine, beer, cider; alcohol in allergy season |
| Stuffy nose with a red face | Acetaldehyde build-up | Any alcohol, often after one drink |
| Wheezing or chest tightness | Airway reaction, not just the nose | Sulfites, AERD, true allergy (needs care) |

## Runny Nose After Drinking

A runny nose after a glass or two is the classic histamine response. Histamine tells the glands in your nose to make more watery mucus and makes small vessels leak fluid into the tissue. That's why the drip is usually thin and clear, rather than the thick mucus you get with a cold.

If your nose runs mainly with wine and less with spirits, histamine and other fermentation compounds are the likely reason. Some people also get a runny nose from the temperature change of a cold drink or a cold beer, much like the drip you get going outside on a winter day. That's a reflex response from the nerves in your nose rather than an allergy, and it settles on its own.

## Sneezing After Drinking

Sneezing comes from histamine irritating the nerve endings inside your nose. Some people sneeze a few times after the first sip of wine or beer and then stop. Others sneeze on and off all evening.

If you already have hay fever or a dust or pet allergy, you're more likely to sneeze when you drink, because your nose is already primed to react and alcohol adds to the histamine load. Many people notice their alcohol-related sneezing is worse in spring or late summer, when pollen is high. That's a useful clue: if your symptoms flare in allergy season and calm down the rest of the year, alcohol is probably adding to an existing allergy rather than causing a new one.

## Stuffy Nose After Drinking Wine

Wine is the drink people most often link to nasal symptoms, and population surveys of people with alcohol-triggered nose and airway symptoms have consistently found wine to be the most common trigger, with red wine leading the way. Several things stack up in a glass of red:

- **Histamine and other biogenic amines** from fermentation, generally higher in red than in white.
- **Sulfites**, used as a preservative in most wines.
- **Compounds from grape skins**, which red wine has much more contact with.
- **Higher alcohol content** than beer, so more vessel widening per glass.

If red wine reliably blocks your nose but white wine and spirits don't, you've learned something useful about your own triggers. Many people with this pattern also get headaches from red wine, which we cover in our guide to [red wine headaches](/never-hungover/red-wine-headache). Sparkling wine bothers some people quickly, possibly because the bubbles speed up alcohol absorption, though that's mostly based on how people describe their own experience rather than solid research.

## Stuffy Nose After Drinking Beer

Beer is the second common trigger. It's fermented, so it contains histamine, and it brings extra ingredients that wine doesn't: barley or wheat, hops, and live or residual yeast in some styles. Unfiltered, cloudy, and sour beers tend to carry more fermentation by-products than filtered lagers.

If you only react to beer, it's worth noticing whether it's all beer or just certain styles. Reacting to every beer but not to wine or spirits can occasionally point to a sensitivity to a grain or to hops, and an allergist can test for those. Reacting mainly to craft, wheat, or unfiltered beers points more toward fermentation compounds. Gluten-free beers aren't automatically better for your nose, since they still contain histamine from fermentation.

## Does Alcohol Make Sinus Problems and Nasal Polyps Worse?

Yes, for many people. If you already have chronic sinus inflammation, the nasal lining is swollen most of the time, and alcohol's effect on blood vessels can be enough to block it completely. People with long-term sinus problems often report that drinking makes their symptoms worse for a day or more.

There's one condition worth knowing about by name. **Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD)**, also called Samter's triad, is a combination of asthma, nasal polyps, and reactions to aspirin and similar painkillers such as ibuprofen. Research from AERD specialty clinics has found that most people with the condition also get nose and chest symptoms from alcohol, often from small amounts. If you have nasal polyps or asthma and you've ever had a bad reaction to aspirin or ibuprofen, mention your alcohol reactions to your doctor. It's a pattern that's often missed, and it has specific treatments.

## Is It an Alcohol Allergy or an Intolerance?

Most people who search for this are worried they're allergic to alcohol. In the vast majority of cases, they're not.

- **Intolerance** means your body handles something in the drink poorly: histamine, sulfites, or acetaldehyde. It's uncomfortable but not dangerous in the way allergies can be. Nasal stuffiness, flushing, and headaches are typical. Our guide to [alcohol intolerance](/never-hungover/alcohol-intolerance) explains the main types and how they're tested.
- **A true allergy** is an immune reaction to a specific ingredient, such as grapes, a grain, hops, or yeast. A genuine allergy to ethanol itself is extremely rare. Allergic reactions can include hives, swelling, wheezing, and in rare cases anaphylaxis, a severe reaction that affects breathing and blood pressure. See our guide to [alcohol allergy](/never-hungover/alcohol-allergy) for how to tell the two apart.

A stuffy or runny nose on its own, without hives, swelling, or breathing trouble, is almost always intolerance or a simple vessel effect. That doesn't make it unimportant, but it does mean the usual answer is adjusting what and how much you drink rather than avoiding alcohol out of fear.

## How to Stop a Stuffy Nose From Drinking

### Before and while you drink

- **Notice your trigger drink.** Keep a simple note for a few weeks: what you drank, how much, and whether your nose reacted. Patterns usually show up fast.
- **Choose lower-histamine options.** Clear spirits such as vodka, gin, or white rum with soda water or a simple mixer usually cause fewer symptoms than red wine or unfiltered beer. If you want wine, many people do better with white or rosé than red, though bottles vary.
- **Drink less, and slower.** Vessel widening and histamine build-up both rise with the amount you drink. Sipping slowly and alternating with water gives your body more time to clear acetaldehyde and histamine.
- **Eat first.** Food slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream, which can blunt the quick spike in symptoms.
- **Be careful in allergy season.** If pollen already has your nose on edge, a drink is more likely to push it over. Having your usual allergy treatment under control helps.

### After symptoms start

- **Saline spray or a saline rinse.** This is the safest first step. It thins mucus and washes out irritants, and it doesn't interact with alcohol.
- **Warm steam.** A hot shower or breathing steam from a bowl of hot water can loosen things up for a while.
- **Stay hydrated.** Water won't fix histamine, but alcohol makes you lose fluid, and dry nasal passages feel worse.
- **Raise your head at night.** An extra pillow helps keep blood from pooling in your nasal tissue.
- **Stop drinking for the night.** Symptoms usually fade within a few hours once your body has cleared the alcohol.

## Antihistamines, Decongestants, and Nasal Sprays With Alcohol

Medicines can help, but this is where you need to be careful, because several common ones interact with alcohol. **Talk to a pharmacist or doctor before combining any of these with drinking**, especially if you take other medicines or have a health condition.

- **Older antihistamines** such as diphenhydramine (Benadryl), chlorpheniramine, and doxylamine cause strong drowsiness. Alcohol adds to that sedation, slows your reactions, and can make breathing shallower in large amounts. Avoid combining them with alcohol.
- **Newer, less-sedating antihistamines** such as loratadine and fexofenadine cause less drowsiness, and cetirizine sits in between. Alcohol can still make you sleepier than expected. Our guide to [antihistamines and alcohol](/never-hungover/antihistamines-and-alcohol) covers each one.
- **Antihistamines don't fix acetaldehyde build-up.** If your blocked nose comes with flushing, an antihistamine may hide the redness while the acetaldehyde stays high. We explain this in detail in [antihistamines for alcohol intolerance](/never-hungover/antihistamines-for-alcohol-intolerance).
- **Oral decongestants** such as pseudoephedrine can raise heart rate and blood pressure and keep you awake. Alcohol already speeds up the heart and disrupts sleep, so the two can stack. Skip them if you have high blood pressure, heart problems, or an anxiety disorder, and ask a pharmacist first otherwise. Phenylephrine, the decongestant in many "PE" products, was found by an FDA advisory panel in 2023 to be ineffective when taken by mouth.
- **Medicated nasal sprays** such as oxymetazoline (Afrin) open the nose within minutes, but using them more than about three days in a row can cause rebound congestion that's worse than the original problem.
- **Steroid nasal sprays** such as fluticasone take several days of regular use to work well, so they don't help on the night. If you have ongoing allergy or sinus symptoms that drinking makes worse, a doctor may suggest one as daily treatment.

Never take a sleeping pill or sedating antihistamine to "sleep off" congestion after a night of heavy drinking.

## Why It Feels Worse When You Lie Down

Many people notice their nose is fine at the bar and blocked the moment they get into bed. Lying flat lets more blood pool in the head and nasal tissue, so swelling that was mild while you were upright becomes noticeable. Alcohol also relaxes the muscles at the back of the throat, which is why people tend to snore more after drinking, and a blocked nose makes you breathe through your mouth, which dries out your throat.

The result is lighter, more broken sleep. Alcohol already disrupts the second half of the night, and nasal congestion adds to that. If you often wake at 3 or 4 a.m. after drinking, our guide to [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains what's happening. If you've been told you stop breathing or gasp in your sleep, mention it to a doctor, because alcohol can make sleep apnea worse.

## When a Stuffy Nose Is a Sign of Something More

For most social drinkers, an occasional stuffy nose after wine is a nuisance, not a warning. A few patterns are worth taking more seriously:

- **Symptoms that move to your chest.** Wheezing, coughing, or chest tightness after drinking suggests your airways are reacting, not just your nose. This is more common in people with asthma and in people sensitive to sulfites, and it should be discussed with a doctor.
- **Swelling, hives, or trouble breathing.** These suggest a true allergic reaction. Get emergency care right away, especially if symptoms are getting worse quickly.
- **Reactions to tiny amounts.** If a few sips cause a strong reaction, or it's a new problem that appeared suddenly, see a doctor. New alcohol intolerance can occasionally be linked to medicines you've started or to other health conditions.
- **A blocked nose that never fully clears.** If you're stuffy most days and alcohol just makes it worse, the real issue may be chronic sinus inflammation, nasal polyps, or allergies that deserve their own treatment.
- **A constant red, blocked nose and facial redness.** Regular drinking can worsen rosacea, a skin condition that causes facial redness and visible blood vessels. A dermatologist can help.

## A Note on DHM

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's studied mainly for how it may affect alcohol metabolism and next-day symptoms. Most of that research is in animals and lab models, with limited human data. **There is no good evidence that DHM prevents or treats nasal congestion from drinking**, and it is not an antihistamine or a decongestant. If your nose is your main complaint, choosing lower-histamine drinks and drinking less will do far more.

If you're interested in DHM for the morning after, read our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) first and check it against any medicines you take. Popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the single-ingredient [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Neither makes it safe to drink more, and neither replaces the advice above.

## The Bottom Line

A stuffy, runny, or sneezy nose after drinking is usually caused by alcohol widening the blood vessels in your nose and by histamine, both the histamine in fermented drinks and the extra your body releases in response to alcohol. Red wine is the most common trigger, beer comes next, and clear spirits tend to cause the fewest problems. Drinking less, choosing your drinks carefully, and using saline are the safest fixes. Be cautious with antihistamines and decongestants, which interact with alcohol, and get help right away if your symptoms ever include wheezing, swelling, hives, or trouble breathing.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does my nose get stuffy when I drink alcohol?**

Usually for two overlapping reasons. Alcohol widens blood vessels, including the ones lining the inside of your nose, and that swelling narrows the airway. On top of that, histamine (found naturally in wine and beer, and also released by your own body in response to alcohol and its by-product acetaldehyde) makes those vessels leak fluid and triggers mucus. The result is a blocked or runny nose that often starts within minutes of the first drink.

**Why do I sneeze or get a runny nose after drinking wine?**

Wine is one of the most commonly reported triggers. It contains histamine and other biogenic amines produced during fermentation, red wine generally more than white, plus sulfites and grape-skin compounds that bother some people. Alcohol also slows the breakdown of histamine and makes nasal blood vessels swell, so the histamine you drink and the histamine you release add together. Sneezing and a runny nose are classic histamine effects.

**Is a stuffy nose after drinking an alcohol allergy?**

Almost never. A true allergy to ethanol is very rare. Most people with nasal symptoms after drinking have an intolerance or sensitivity: a reaction to histamine, sulfites, or other ingredients, or a slow ability to clear acetaldehyde. A real allergy to an ingredient (such as grapes, wheat, barley, or hops) is possible but uncommon. Hives, swelling of the lips or tongue, wheezing, or trouble breathing are not ordinary congestion and need urgent care.

**Which alcohol is least likely to cause a stuffy nose?**

Clear, distilled spirits such as vodka, gin, or white rum mixed with a plain mixer tend to cause the fewest nasal symptoms for most people, because distillation leaves behind most of the histamine and other fermentation compounds. Red wine, then beer and white wine, are the most common triggers. Alcohol itself still widens blood vessels, so even clear spirits can cause some stuffiness, especially in larger amounts.

**Can I take an antihistamine for a stuffy nose from drinking?**

Some people do, but talk to a doctor or pharmacist first, especially if you take other medicines. Older antihistamines such as diphenhydramine (Benadryl) are strongly sedating and should not be combined with alcohol. Newer ones such as loratadine or fexofenadine are less sedating, but alcohol can still increase drowsiness. If you get facial flushing as well, an antihistamine can hide the flush without changing the acetaldehyde build-up behind it.

**Is it safe to use a decongestant after drinking?**

Saline spray or rinses are the safest first step. Oral decongestants such as pseudoephedrine can raise heart rate and blood pressure and make it harder to sleep, which stacks on top of alcohol's effects on the heart and sleep, so ask a pharmacist before combining them, and avoid them if you have high blood pressure or heart problems. Medicated sprays like oxymetazoline work quickly but should not be used for more than about three days in a row, because they can cause rebound congestion.

**Why is my nose stuffier at night after drinking?**

Lying flat lets more blood pool in the nasal tissues, so congestion that was mild while you were upright often gets worse in bed. Alcohol also relaxes the muscles of the throat, which is why people tend to snore more after drinking. Raising your head slightly, rinsing with saline before bed, and stopping drinking a few hours before sleep can help.

**When should I see a doctor about nasal symptoms after drinking?**

Book a regular appointment if it happens every time you drink, if it is getting worse, if you also have asthma, nasal polyps, or chronic sinus problems, or if you react badly to aspirin or ibuprofen, since that combination can point to a condition called aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease. Get emergency care right away for wheezing, chest tightness, trouble breathing, swelling of the face, lips, or tongue, widespread hives, or feeling faint.

**Does DHM help with a stuffy nose from alcohol?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents or treats alcohol-related nasal congestion, and it is not an antihistamine. DHM is studied mainly for how it may affect alcohol metabolism and next-day symptoms, mostly in animal and lab research with limited human data. If your main problem is congestion, choosing lower-histamine drinks and drinking less will do more.
